title: Operators
summary: The symbols that do the work: arithmetic, comparison, and logic.
refresher: **Operators** are the symbols that combine values. `+ - * /` do arithmetic and `%` gives the remainder. Division is the one to watch: if both sides are `int`, Java divides as **integers** and throws the fraction away, so `7 / 2` is 3. Make one side a `double` to get 3.5. Comparisons like `==` and `<` produce a `boolean`, and `&&`, `||`, and `!` combine those **booleans**. Assignment is `=`. Comparison is `==`. They are different operators.

operators-lesson-check-1.title: Trace arithmetic one line at a time
operators-lesson-check-1.body: This question is about following each **operator** in order. Work out one printed line, write that result down, then move to the next line.
operators-lesson-check-1.notice: `//` keeps the whole-number part, `%` keeps the remainder, and `/` keeps the decimal result.
operators-lesson-check-1.mistake: Do not round floor division. It drops the leftover part instead of rounding up.

operators-lesson-check-2.title: Between means both boundaries count
operators-lesson-check-2.body: A between check asks two questions: high enough and low enough. If both ends count, the comparison needs inclusive operators.
operators-lesson-check-2.notice: `and` means both comparisons must be true at the same time.
operators-lesson-check-2.mistake: `or` is usually too loose for a between rule because one true side is enough to enter.

operators-summary-01.title: Operators do different jobs
operators-summary-01.body: **Operators** calculate values, compare values, assign values, and combine true-or-false conditions. First decide which job the line is doing.
operators-summary-01.notice: Arithmetic makes a value. Comparison makes true or false. Assignment stores a value.
operators-summary-01.mistake: Do not treat every symbol as math. Some operators ask questions or store values.

operators-supplement-01.title: Assignment is not comparison
operators-supplement-01.body: A condition should ask whether something is true. Assignment changes a value; comparison asks whether two values match.
operators-supplement-01.notice: Use the comparison operator when an if statement is asking a yes/no question.
operators-supplement-01.mistake: A single equals sign is a common typo when the code meant to compare.

operators-authored-01.title: Zero cannot be the divisor
operators-authored-01.body: Division, floor division, and remainder all need a nonzero divisor. If the divisor can come from input or another calculation, check it before dividing.
operators-authored-01.notice: The dangerous value is the number after the division or remainder operator.
operators-authored-01.mistake: Do not assume a calculated count is safe just because the formula looks reasonable.

operators-authored-02.title: Choose storing or comparing
operators-authored-02.body: Before reading a conditional expression, ask whether the code is storing a new value or comparing existing values.
operators-authored-02.notice: Assignment changes state. Comparison produces a true-or-false answer.
operators-authored-02.mistake: Mixing these up can either stop the program or quietly send it down the wrong branch.

operators-authored-03.title: Pick the division that matches the problem
operators-authored-03.body: Division operators answer different questions. Use decimal division for averages, whole-number division for complete groups, and remainder for what is left.
operators-authored-03.example:
groups = students // seats
left = students % seats
operators-authored-03.notice: The same two numbers can produce different useful answers depending on the operator.
operators-authored-03.mistake: Do not use whole-number division when the assignment expects a decimal average.

operators-authored-04.title: Floor division drops the leftover
operators-authored-04.body: Whole-number division keeps the number of complete groups and ignores the leftover part.
operators-authored-04.notice: The leftover is not lost forever if the code also asks for the remainder.
operators-authored-04.mistake: Do not round up. Complete groups only count when they are fully filled.

operators-authored-05.title: Remainder checks divisibility
operators-authored-05.body: The remainder operator is useful when a rule depends on whether something divides evenly.
operators-authored-05.notice: Even numbers leave remainder 0 when divided by 2.
operators-authored-05.mistake: Do not compare the original number to 0 when the question is about the leftover.

operators-authored-06.title: Power has its own operator
operators-authored-06.body: When a question asks about raising a number to a power, look for the language's exponent operator or function, not a symbol that only looks mathematical.
operators-authored-06.notice: A familiar-looking symbol can mean something different in code.
operators-authored-06.mistake: Do not assume `^` means exponent just because it is used that way in some calculators or notes.

sections.title: Mathematical operators
sections.summary: Use arithmetic symbols, remainder, and integer division carefully.

blocks.body: An **operator** is a symbol that works with values. Java uses `+`, `-`, and `*` for add, subtract, and multiply. Division needs extra care, and so does telling `=` apart from `==`.

blocks.caption: `%` gives the remainder after division. `7 / 2` is 3, and `7 % 2` is 1. The examples below focus on the statements inside the usual Java wrapper.

blocks.body: Look at that third line again. `7 / 2` gave you 3, not 3.5. Java did not round it. It threw the fraction away and kept the whole number. That is **integer division**, and it is doing exactly what it was told to do.

blocks.title: Integer division truncates
blocks.body: When both sides of `/` are **integers**, Java keeps only the whole-number part. `7 / 2` is 3 and `9 / 10` is 0. If an average looks too low, look for int divided by int.

blocks.caption: The types going in decide the type coming out. One `double` in the division is enough to keep the fraction. `(double) total` casts total for this expression.

blocks.prompt: The result is stored in a `double`, so what does this **print**?
blocks.why: Java works out `total / count` on its own, before it ever looks at the left side. Both are `int`, so that is **integer division** and the answer is 3. Only then is the 3 stored in a `double`, which turns it into 3.0. The fraction was already gone by that point. If you picked 3.5, you assumed the `double` on the left reaches back and changes how the division is done. It does not. The type on the left says where the answer goes, not how it gets computed. Writing `(double) total / count` fixes it.

sections.title: Update shortcuts
sections.summary: Use +=, -=, ++, and -- only when they make state changes clearer.

blocks.caption: Java gives you shortcuts for updating a **variable** from its own current **value**. `score += 3` is short for `score = score + 3`, and `score++` adds exactly 1. Each line changes the variable in place, so the prints let you watch it move: 5 becomes 8, then 9, then back down to 5.

blocks.title: x++ and ++x are not always the same
blocks.body: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, and `%=` update a variable in place. `x++` adds 1 and `x--` subtracts 1. If `++` appears inside a larger expression, split it into two lines so the order is clear.

sections.title: Bitwise operators
sections.summary: Recognize the operators that work on integer bits and flags.

blocks.body: Java also has **bitwise operators** for the individual **bits** inside integers. `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, and `>>` are useful for masks and low-level flags. They are not the operators you normally use to join `boolean` conditions.

blocks.caption: These examples work on integer bit patterns. `&` keeps shared 1 bits, `|` keeps any 1 bit, `^` keeps differing bits, and `<<` shifts left, which multiplies by powers of two for positive integers.

blocks.title: Do not confuse & with &&
blocks.body: For normal **conditions**, use `&&` for and and `||` for or. A single `&` or `|` can compile in some boolean expressions, but it does not short-circuit and is usually not what a beginner exercise wants. Count the symbols when a condition behaves strangely.

sections.title: Comparison and assignment
sections.summary: Make sure an if statement receives a boolean question, not an assigned number.

blocks.body: The next group asks questions instead of doing math. A comparison **operator** takes two **values** and produces a `boolean`, which is either `true` or `false`. That is the type an `if` statement needs.

blocks.caption: `==` asks whether two **values** match, and `!=` asks whether they differ. You also get `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=`. Each one hands back a **boolean**, and a boolean is an ordinary value, which is why you can **print** it straight out without an `if` anywhere in sight.
Logical **operators** join booleans. `&&` means both sides must be true. `||` means either side can be true. `!` flips the value. Use the doubled symbols for normal boolean logic.
`=` assigns a **value**. `==` compares two values. An `if` needs a boolean, so `if (score = 5)` fails because assignment produces an int, not true or false.

blocks.title: Java catches this at compile time, with one exception
blocks.body: Java catches `if (score = 5)` before running. A boolean variable is trickier: `if (done = true)` compiles because it assigns true and then tests true. If a **condition** seems stuck, count the equals signs.

sections.title: Conditional logic and precedence
sections.summary: Combine boolean conditions and use parentheses when an expression gets dense.

blocks.body: **Precedence** means which operator runs first. Java does multiplication, division, and remainder before addition and subtraction. Parentheses make the order clear, and they are always allowed.

blocks.why: Take it one line at a time. `x` starts at 10, and `x += 5` makes it 15. Then `15 / 3` is an int divided by an int, and this one happens to come out even, so the answer is 5 and no fraction is lost. It prints as `5` rather than `5.0` because int division produces an `int`, and Java prints an int with no decimal point. If you picked 5.0, you were watching for the truncation trap, which is the right instinct aimed at the wrong line. The trap costs you nothing here, because 15 divides by 3 exactly.

blocks.title: What to check when the arithmetic looks wrong
items: An average or a percentage came out too low, or came out as 0: you divided an `int` by an `int`. Cast one side with `(double)`.
Declaring the result as a `double` does not rescue you. `double avg = 7 / 2;` is 3.0, because the division finished before the assignment happened.
A **condition** never changes: count the equals signs. `=` assigns, `==` compares.
Use `%` to test divisibility. `n % 2 == 0` is how you ask whether n is even.
When one expression mixes `*`, `+`, and `&&`, add parentheses. They cost nothing and they say what you meant.
The compiler checks types before your code runs, so an error it catches is the cheapest bug you will get. The expensive ones are the lines that compile and still give you the wrong number.
